opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm optimistic for a few reasons, and the first is that I've spent most of my career actually trying to get robots to do things, and that gives you a pretty humbling view of where the technology really is.

There's a huge gap between the demos people see online and what robots can reliably do in the real world. Take something as simple as picking up an object you've never seen before, or folding laundry, or clearing a dinner table. Humans do these things effortlessly. A three-year-old can do them. For robots, they're still extraordinarily hard. This is Moravec's paradox: the things we find hard, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers, and the things we find trivial, like perception and manipulation, are fiendishly difficult. We've made real progress, especially in the last few years, but robust dexterity in unstructured environments is still a long way off. So the fear that robots are about to sweep through and take over all physical work is, I think, quite overblown.

The second reason is historical. Every major wave of automation has come with predictions of mass unemployment, going back to the Luddites and through the mechanization of agriculture. What actually happens, again and again, is that the nature of work changes. Some tasks get automated, but new tasks and new jobs emerge, often ones nobody could have predicted. A hundred years ago most people worked on farms. Nobody then could have imagined a job like "app developer" or "data scientist" or "podcast host."

And the third reason, which is the one I care most about, is that I think the right framing isn't humans versus machines, it's humans with machines. I've been using the word "multiplicity" as a counterpoint to the idea of the singularity. Instead of one superintelligence replacing us, the more realistic and more interesting future is diverse groups of humans and machines working together, each doing what they're good at. Machines are great at repetitive, precise, tireless work. Humans bring judgment, creativity, empathy, adaptability, the ability to handle the weird edge case. When you combine them you get something better than either alone.

There's also a demographic piece people overlook. In many countries, populations are aging and workforces are shrinking. We're going to need help, in elder care, in logistics, in agriculture, in construction. In that context, robots aren't so much taking jobs as filling gaps that we genuinely don't have enough people for.

Now, I don't want to be Pollyannaish. Transitions can be painful, and specific workers and communities can get hurt even when the overall picture is fine. That's real, and we need good policy, retraining, and support to handle it. But the narrative that the robots are coming for all our jobs, I just don't think the evidence supports it. If anything, I think we'll be working alongside these systems for a very long time.

r001.rationale: The response says humans contribute judgment, creativity, empathy, adaptability, and the ability to handle unusual edge cases, explaining why they remain useful alongside machines.

r002.rationale: It says some tasks will be automated and work will change, but does not state that this frees workers to focus more on other aspects of their jobs.

r003.rationale: It cites aging populations and shrinking workforces, then says robots will fill genuine staffing gaps rather than mainly take jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been working on robots for a long time, and I'd say the biggest thing people get wrong is how hard the physical world actually is. We've had this idea since the 1950s that robots are about to take over all the factories and the warehouses, and it keeps not happening. There's something I call Moravec's paradox, which goes back decades: things that are hard for humans, like playing chess or doing calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for machines, and things that are easy for humans, like picking up a coffee cup or folding a towel, turn out to be enormously hard for robots.

So right now robots are still terrible at grasping. A child can pick up almost any object you hand them. Our best robots still fumble with a surprising fraction of objects in a bin. Every dexterous task a human does involves perception, sensing, planning, feedback, all of it running continuously, and it's remarkably hard to replicate. And so when I look at the labor market, I see a huge amount of work that involves physical manipulation in unstructured environments. Plumbers, electricians, nurses, caregivers, people doing construction. I don't see those jobs going away for a very long time.

The other piece is that I think people underestimate the complementarity. In the factories I visit, the robots and the humans work side by side. The robot does the heavy, repetitive, dangerous part, and the humans do the parts that require judgment and dexterity. What I've seen historically is that automation tends to shift jobs rather than eliminate them. When ATMs came in, the number of bank tellers actually went up for a couple decades, because branches became cheaper to open. I'm not saying there's no disruption, there clearly is, and we should take it seriously. But I think the narrative of mass unemployment driven by robots is way ahead of the actual technology.

And honestly, there's a demographic side to this too. In Japan, in Europe, in the US, we have aging populations and labor shortages in exactly the sectors where we'd want help. Warehouses can't hire enough people. Hospitals can't hire enough nurses. So I see robots filling gaps more than displacing workers, at least over the horizon I can reasonably see. I try to be humble about predictions, because the field has a long history of overpromising. But that history is actually part of why I'm optimistic.

r001.rationale: The response says humans handle factory tasks requiring judgment and dexterity, and points to physical manipulation in unstructured environments as work robots will struggle to replace.

r002.rationale: It describes robots doing heavy, repetitive, dangerous work while humans do judgment and dexterity tasks, but does not state that automation frees workers to give more attention to other parts of their jobs.

r003.rationale: It links aging populations and labor shortages to its expectation that robots will fill gaps more than displace workers over the foreseeable horizon.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic because automating a task isn’t the same thing as automating a job. Most jobs involve a whole collection of activities, and some of the things people do almost without thinking—handling an unexpected situation, understanding what someone needs, working in an unfamiliar environment—are still very difficult for robots.

So I think there’s a lot of potential for people and machines to complement each other. A machine can take over a repetitive part of the work, while the person brings judgment and adaptability. That can make people more productive and open up opportunities that are difficult to anticipate today.

But optimism doesn’t mean the transition will be painless. Someone whose job disappears needs a real path to another livelihood. We have to take training and support seriously. My optimism is about what the technology can enable; whether that translates into better jobs depends on the choices we make.

r001.rationale: It says people handle unexpected situations, understand others’ needs, and adapt in unfamiliar environments—tasks that remain difficult for robots.

r002.rationale: It says machines can take over repetitive work while people contribute judgment and adaptability, but does not state that automation frees workers to give more attention to other aspects of their jobs.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute limited future automation-driven unemployment to a shortage of working-age people.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic because automating a task is different from automating a job. Most jobs involve a whole collection of tasks, and some of those are much harder to automate than others. Robots can be very good at a narrowly defined activity, but dealing with an unexpected situation, understanding what somebody needs, or working in an unfamiliar environment is still challenging.

So I think there’s a lot of room for people and machines to complement each other. If a robot takes over the repetitive or dangerous part of your work, that can make your judgment and your ability to work with other people more valuable. It can also make products and services less expensive, which creates opportunities to do more of them.

That doesn’t mean the transition will be painless. People can lose jobs, and the new opportunities won’t necessarily appear in the same place or require the same skills. We have to take that seriously. But I don’t think we should assume that there’s a fixed amount of work and that every task a machine does leaves less for a person. We’re very good at finding new things we want to do.

r001.rationale: It points to human strengths such as handling unexpected situations, understanding people’s needs, and working in unfamiliar environments as reasons people complement automated tasks.

r002.rationale: It says automation can make human judgment and collaboration more valuable, but does not clearly say it frees workers to give more attention to other job duties.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute an expectation about future automation-driven unemployment to a shortage of working-age people.
